lines.text: # Starting the optional OWS match at the beginning of a whitespace run avoids
# quadratic backtracking for long header values.
# Keep the original message in sync for downstream consumers such as
# cookie jars while preserving its identity and header ordering.
def test_normalize_header_value(self, value: str, expected: str) -> None:
"\r" not in value and "\n" not in value for value in r.headers.values()
Fixed response header handling to replace obsolete folded header lines
(`obs-fold`) with spaces in accordance with RFC 9112, preventing raw
CRLF sequences from appearing in header values such as ``Set-Cookie``.

description.html:
Unfold obsolete folded response headers

Addresses the original obs-fold response-header case discussed in #1362. Python's http.client preserves obsolete folded response header lines in HTTPMessage values. This change replaces each RFC 9112 OWS CRLF RWS sequence with a single space before urllib3 or downstream consumers interpret the value.

The normalization

  • keeps urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict and the original HTTPMessage synchronized, preventing cookie consumers such as Requests from re-emitting raw CRLF;
  • preserves header names, ordering, duplicate fields, and parser state;
  • uses a common-case fast path and a linear-time pattern for long field values.

Tests

The socket regression covers the original folded Set-Cookie, duplicate cookies, every SP/HTAB combination around CRLF, mixed and repeated whitespace, multiple folds, and ordinary headers. Focused unit coverage also verifies adjacent folds and preservation of the original message's order, duplicates, payload, policy, and defects.

This intentionally does not address the separate whitespace-before-colon/header name validation scope discussed on #1362.

Validation performed

  • full local suite: 2,279 passed, 333 skipped, 4 xfailed;
  • focused strict nox sessions on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14;
  • pyupgrade, Black, isort, and flake8;
  • towncrier changelog validation;
  • source distribution and wheel builds;
  • end-to-end Requests cookie extraction and subsequent request serialization.

text.standard: HTTP/1.1 used to let a server continue a header value on the next line by starting that line with a space or tab. That's obsolete line folding. Python's http.client keeps the folded value as it arrived, with the raw CRLF inside it, and urllib3 copied those values straight into its HTTPHeaderDict. A header such as Set-Cookie could therefore contain a hidden line break.
text.simple: Old servers sometimes split one header across two lines. Python keeps the line break inside the header's value, and urllib3 passed it along unchanged, so some header values contained hidden line breaks.
text.deep: A parser leaking its input format. A fold is an encoding detail: one value written across lines. RFC 9112 requires a recipient to replace each fold with spaces before interpreting the value. Keeping the CRLF lets the wire format leak into the value itself, and every consumer then has to unfold it again, or carries the line break further.

text.standard: The line break isn't just untidy. Libraries that copy cookies from the response, such as Requests, read http.client's own message object and can send the value back out with the raw CRLF in it. That can split one header into two on the next request: header injection. Issue #1362 tracked the original report.
text.simple: Worse, other libraries copy these values into the next request, and the hidden line break can turn one header into two.
text.deep: A safety property. A header value must never contain CR or LF once it leaves the parser, because anything that writes it out again treats the line break as the end of the header. Normalizing at the one point where urllib3 turns the parsed response into its own types fixes every consumer at once, as long as the original message is fixed too.

text.standard: urllib3 now unfolds header values right after http.client parses the response, as restated in the problem. A new helper replaces each fold (optional whitespace, CRLF, then at least one space or tab) with a single space. It updates both urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict and the original HTTPMessage, so code reading either one sees the same clean values.
text.simple: Right after a response arrives, urllib3 now turns every split header back into one line, in both copies of the headers.
text.deep: Normalize the source, then derive. The fix rewrites the HTTPMessage in place (same object, same order, same duplicates) and builds HTTPHeaderDict from the same normalized list. Both views are equal by construction, and nothing downstream has to know folding ever existed.

text.standard: The rule behind it: a parsed header value must never contain a line break. The pattern starts its optional whitespace match only at the beginning of a run of spaces, which keeps it linear-time on long values, and a fast path skips any value without CRLF, which is almost all of them.
text.simple: No header value should contain a line break after parsing. The code also stays fast, even for very long or unusual values.
text.deep: Two properties are enforced together: a semantic one (no CR or LF in values) and a performance one (cost linear in input). The second matters because response headers are attacker-controlled input; a pattern that backtracks quadratically would turn a cleanup step into a denial-of-service vector.

blocks.caption: Where a response's headers go after parsing, and the one place they are now unfolded.

items.html: http.client parses the response headers into an HTTPMessage. A folded value keeps its CRLF and leading whitespace.
getresponse() passes that message to _normalize_header_values instead of reading .items() directly.
Each value goes through _normalize_header_value: values without CRLF return at once, folded ones are rewritten with the pattern.
If any value changed, the message is rewritten in place: every header is deleted, then the normalized list is added back in the same order.
HTTPHeaderDict is built from the same normalized list, so r.headers and r._original_response.msg agree.

items.label: What happens to a fold that ends in a bare LF?

cards.title: Design: why the original HTTPMessage is rewritten too

text.standard: A response's headers exist twice: urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict and http.client's HTTPMessage. Requests reads cookies from the second, so cleaning only the first would leave the raw CRLF where it does harm.

The helper therefore rewrites the original message in place. It keeps the object's identity (the socket test checks headers is msg), its defects and policy, its payload, and the order of every header, including duplicate Set-Cookie lines.
The alternative, building a new message, would break anything already holding a reference to the old one. Normalizing the list once and deriving both views from it makes them equal by construction.

items.label: Is mutating the message in place safe?
What does this cost per response?

cards.title: The pattern: why the lookbehind matters

text.standard: _OBSOLETE_FOLD_RE = (?:(?<![ \t])[ \t]+)?\r\n[ \t]+

items.html: (?:…)?: optional whitespace before the line break, the OWS in OWS CRLF RWS.
(?<![ \t]): that optional whitespace may only start where the previous character isn't a space or tab, i.e. at the start of a run.
[ \t]+: at least one space or tab starting the continuation line, the RWS.

text.standard: Without the lookbehind, a long run of spaces that isn't followed by CRLF makes the engine try every start position and rescan the run each time, which is quadratic. With it, positions inside a run fail at once, so the scan is linear.

items.html: Unfolds exactly the RFC shape: optional whitespace, CRLF, at least one space or tab.
Folds that end in a bare LF are not unfolded.
Order and duplicate headers are preserved when the message is rewritten.
The original message keeps its identity, payload, defects and policy.
The linear-time claim has no test.
Tabs inside ordinary values are left alone.
Two adjacent folds give two spaces, which RFC 9112 allows.

pages.title: Folds that end in a bare LF are not unfolded
pages.summary: http.client accepts header lines ending in LF alone, but the new code only looks for CRLF.

text.standard: Code: the fast path returns early unless the value contains "\r\n", and the pattern requires \r\n.
Parser: http.client accepts header lines ending in a bare LF. Checked locally: parsing Set-Cookie: a=1\n b=2 returns the value 'a=1\n b=2', which these helpers leave unchanged.
Tests: every fold in the socket test and the unit tests uses CRLF.

The invariant the PR states, no raw line breaks in header values, still fails for a folded value whose lines end in a bare LF. That's the same header injection risk through LF instead of CRLF. RFC 9112 lets recipients accept a bare LF as a line terminator, and http.client does. Broadening the pattern and fast path to \r?\n, plus one test, would close it. Confidence is medium: the maintainers may have left LF out deliberately, and it depends on http.client's behaviour.
text.simple: A rarer kind of split header, using only LF, still keeps its line break. A small change to the pattern would cover it.
text.deep: A sanitizer is only as strong as its coverage of the parser it follows: whatever line terminators the parser accepts, the sanitizer must also recognize. Here the parser is more permissive (CRLF or LF) than the sanitizer (CRLF only), so there's a gap between "accepted" and "cleaned".

items.label: Would rejecting folds be safer than unfolding?

pages.title: The linear-time claim has no test
pages.summary: The description and a comment rely on the pattern being linear-time, but nothing would catch a regression.

text.standard: Description: it says the normalization uses a linear-time pattern for long field values.
Code: a comment explains that starting the whitespace match at the beginning of a run avoids quadratic backtracking.
Tests: no test uses a long value or a long run of spaces.

The pattern is correct today, but the property that makes it safe (the lookbehind) is easy to "simplify" away later, and response headers are untrusted input. A test that normalizes a value with a very long run of spaces, kept within a generous time limit, would protect it. This is a test gap, not a bug.

HTTP/1.1 originally let a server continue a header value on the next line, as long as that line started with a space or tab. That's line folding. RFC 9112 now calls it obs-fold (obsolete folding): servers must not send it, and a client that receives it must replace each fold with one or more spaces before using the value. Python's http.client doesn't do that; it keeps the CRLF and the leading whitespace inside the value.
text.simple: Some servers split one long header across two lines, starting the second line with spaces. The modern rule is: treat that split as a single space. Python keeps the line break instead, so urllib3 has to clean it up.
text.deep: A fold is a property of the encoding, not of the value: the same value can be sent folded or not. A parser that keeps the fold leaks its input format into the semantic value, so every consumer must either re-implement unfolding or carry a raw line break further. RFC 9112 section 5.2 resolves it at the recipient, before interpretation or forwarding.

inner.code:
Set-Cookie: a=1; path=/ <CR><LF>
    Max-Age=900<CR><LF>

# http.client keeps:   'a=1; path=/ \r\n    Max-Age=900'
# urllib3 now returns: 'a=1; path=/ Max-Age=900'

text.standard: RFC 9112 allows a recipient to reject a folded message or unfold it. urllib3 unfolds, using one space per fold. Whitespace is one of the OWS and RWS rules.

A urllib3 response carries its headers twice. r.headers is urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict, a case-insensitive dict that keeps repeated headers. r._original_response.msg is the HTTPMessage that http.client built while parsing, based on Python's email message class. urllib3 builds the first from the second, but some libraries, notably Requests for cookies, read the second directly. Fixing only one would leave them disagreeing.
text.simple: There are two copies of the headers: urllib3's own, and the one Python's HTTP library made. Other libraries read different copies, so both need the same clean values.
text.deep: Two representations of one fact are a consistency hazard. The PR chooses to normalize the source, then derive: it rewrites the HTTPMessage in place (keeping the object's identity, defects and policy) and builds HTTPHeaderDict from the same normalized list, so both views are equal by construction.

inner.code:
r = pool.request("GET", "/")
r.headers.getlist("set-cookie")                # urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict
r._original_response.msg.get_all("set-cookie") # http.client's HTTPMessage
# Requests' cookie jar reads the second one.

text.standard: Repeated headers matter here, especially Set-Cookie, which can't be joined into one value.

pages.title: Header injection through raw line breaks

text.standard: HTTP separates headers with CRLF. If a header value itself contains CRLF and some code later writes that value back out, for example a cookie jar sending a stored cookie on the next request, the line break ends the header early and whatever follows becomes a new header. That's header injection. Here the risk is that a folded Set-Cookie could be re-sent with a raw CRLF inside it.
text.simple: A hidden line break inside a header can split one header into two when the value is sent again. Removing line breaks from values prevents that.
text.deep: The invariant is simple: no CR or LF in a field value after parsing. Code that serializes headers trusts that invariant, so it must hold at the boundary where external bytes become values. Enforcing it once in getresponse() protects every downstream serializer, as long as the enforcement covers every line terminator the parser accepts.

inner.code:
# stored cookie value with a raw fold:
"session=abc \r\n X-Injected: 1"
# re-sent as a request header:
Cookie: session=abc
 X-Injected: 1        <- a server may read this as a new header

text.standard: Requests is one such consumer: it reads cookies from the original message.

The pattern is (?:(?<![ \t])[ \t]+)?\r\n[ \t]+: optional spaces or tabs, then CRLF, then at least one space or tab. The (?<![ \t]) lookbehind lets the optional whitespace match start only at the beginning of a run of spaces. Without it, a long run of spaces that isn't followed by CRLF makes the engine try every starting position and rescan the whole run from each one, which takes quadratic time.
text.simple: The pattern finds "spaces, line break, spaces". A small extra check stops it re-reading the same spaces over and over, so very long header values can't make it slow.
text.deep: Regex engines that backtrack retry at each start position. With [ \t]*\r\n, a run of n spaces costs n - i steps from position i, which is O(n^2) in total. The lookbehind fails in O(1) everywhere inside a run, so only the run's first character starts the expensive scan, which brings the total to O(n). It's the same idea as anchoring a token to its leftmost position.

pages.title: OWS and RWS: whitespace in HTTP

text.standard: HTTP's grammar names its whitespace. OWS is optional whitespace (zero or more spaces or tabs) and RWS is required whitespace (at least one). A fold is OWS CRLF RWS: maybe some spaces, the line break, then at least one space or tab starting the next line. That's exactly the shape of the PR's regex.
text.simple: "Optional spaces, a line break, then at least one space": that's what a fold looks like, and that's what the code searches for.

text.standard: Set-Cookie is the one header that can't be combined into a comma-separated list, because cookie attributes such as Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2026 … contain commas themselves. urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict still keeps each Set-Cookie line separately (getlist), and the PR has to preserve that, along with the order of duplicate headers, when it rewrites the message.
text.simple: Each cookie has to stay as its own header line, because cookies contain commas. The fix keeps every cookie separate and in order.
text.deep: Set-Cookie breaks the general rule that repeated fields are equivalent to one comma-joined field (RFC 9110 section 5.3 calls this out explicitly). Any header normalization therefore has to work on the list of (name, value) pairs, never on a joined map, which is why the helper takes message.items() and writes them back in order.

text.standard: Requests builds its cookie jar from response._original_response.msg, the http.client message, not from urllib3's r.headers. That's why the PR rewrites the original message in place instead of only cleaning the dict it builds. The socket-level test checks both views and that the message is still the same object.
text.simple: Requests reads cookies from Python's own copy of the headers, so that copy has to be fixed too, not just urllib3's.
